1.1.explanation: Translating a business problem starts with the business outcome, not the model: users, inputs, data boundaries, processing stages, outputs, feedback, and measurable value. The core discipline is splitting the work three ways — what suits language understanding or planning, what an existing system already does reliably, and what a person must retain.
1.1.example: A support organization wants faster ticket resolution. The translation yields a classifier that routes tickets, retrieval over the knowledge base for draft answers, and a human step for refunds — with resolution time as the tracked metric.
1.1.guidance: Start from the outcome and the baseline metric, then justify each model assignment on reversibility, error cost, and accountability. The classic error is handing a deterministic business rule to a probabilistic system.

1.2.explanation: An end-to-end architecture traces one request through ingestion, model calls, tools, validation, delivery, and feedback, with each boundary carrying a trust level, failure mode, fallback, and owner. Feedback loops close the system: outputs are measured and the results shape future behavior.
1.2.example: A document-processing pipeline ingests PDFs, extracts fields with Claude, validates against schema and confidence thresholds, routes low-confidence extractions to reviewers, and feeds corrections back into the prompt and the evaluation set.
1.2.guidance: Draw the request path end to end before choosing components, and annotate every boundary with what happens when it fails. An architecture that cannot say where a request dies is not yet a design.

1.3.explanation: Three shapes sit on one spectrum: a single augmented LLM call, a workflow whose control flow lives in code, and an agent whose control flow lives in the model. Five factors decide in order — predictability, error cost, observability, latency budget, and cost — and the first factor that rules a shape out decides.
1.3.example: A compliant summarization of fixed inputs is a chain with deterministic guards between steps; an open-ended research task with no enumerable path justifies an agent bounded by its toolset and a turn limit.
1.3.guidance: Eliminate by constraint, not preference: enumerate the steps if you can, and prefer the workflow whose guards you wrote. Choosing an agent because work feels open-ended is not the same as being unable to write the steps down.

1.4.explanation: A coordinator owns the goal, decomposes work, and synthesizes; workers each carry one scoped unit in their own context. Multi-agent systems fail asymmetrically — workers fail recoverably at their boundary, while a coordinator losing the goal or the merge state usually loses the run.
1.4.example: An orchestrator splits a codebase audit into per-directory workers, reconciles that completed units match dispatched units, and applies an explicit tie-breaking rule when two workers disagree.
1.4.guidance: Reach for multi-agent only when work genuinely exceeds one context, protect coordinator state with checkpoints, propagate one trace identifier across roles, and reconcile coverage at synthesis before any summary reaches a reader.

1.5.explanation: Decomposition splits a complex task into bounded components with explicit contracts and ownership. It comes before architecture: over-assigning work to the model is the most expensive early mistake and the easiest to defend in a demo.
1.5.example: A contract-analysis request decomposes into clause extraction, comparison against a playbook, and exception review — each with a defined input, output, and owner, so failures localize to one component.
1.5.guidance: Split until each component has a contract you can test and a failure you can name. Where a subtask cannot be bounded, that is the signal for a human step or a narrower problem statement.

1.6.explanation: Value pillars — efficiency, transformation, productivity, solution cost, and performance service levels — are the language the budget holder shares with the blueprint. The case is built as a comparison: measured baseline, projected state in the same unit, minus run cost, expressed as a payback period with sensitivity.
1.6.example: An automation case compares today's measured handle time with the projected state from a sizing model, flags that reviewers still handle part of the volume, and presents payback under best- and worst-case volume.
1.6.guidance: Measure the baseline rather than estimating it, model the automation the design actually ships, and take run cost from the input distribution's tail, not the average. An undocumented constraint becomes an infeasible system the moment production violates it.

2.1.explanation: Model choice matches capability, speed, and cost to each unit of work instead of defaulting every stage to one model. Start at the balanced tier and move on evaluation evidence: up when the default misses the quality bar, down when the eval confirms the trade is acceptable.
2.1.example: A pipeline routes extraction to a stronger model only for low-confidence classifications, after an evaluation showed the balanced tier missing the accuracy bar on exactly that category.
2.1.guidance: Treat a model swap as a release with a curated case set, a grading function, and a rollback threshold agreed before the run. Declining to choose defaults to the most expensive option at every step.

2.2.explanation: A reusable system prompt states role and scope, the constraints that must hold, and an output contract naming the response shape. A well-built template makes the guarded path the path of least resistance: fixed scaffolding carries the guarantees, and filling a slot cannot remove a constraint.
2.2.example: A support-drafting template fixes the sections, embeds the prohibited-claims rule as a structural requirement of the output, and leaves only the ticket body as a filled slot.
2.2.guidance: Express must-hold rules structurally rather than as one more line of role description, because a guardrail written as prose can be drifted past. Spot what the prompt leaves silent — wherever it is silent, the model improvises, differently each time.

2.3.explanation: Use the lightest technique that clears the bar: instruction alone, then examples when showing the shape is easier than specifying it, then explicit step-by-step reasoning only when the path genuinely determines the answer. Every escalation costs tokens and latency on every call.
2.3.example: A structured extraction task passes zero-shot with a schema; an unusual output casing is pinned with one example rather than a paragraph of description.
2.3.guidance: Expect identical wording to behave differently across model tiers and generations — a prompt tuned on one model is a draft for the next. Watch for construction bias: leading phrasing, one-sided example sets, and instructions that presume the answer.

2.4.explanation: Four context mechanisms stay distinct: the window itself (active attention, resets between calls), retrieval (fetches knowledge at query time), application state (lives in your systems, reached by tool call), and memory or summaries (continuity you store and pass back). The window is a ceiling, not a target.
2.4.example: A long-running analyst session carries recent turns, retrieves policy documents on demand, keeps account state behind a tool, and compacts everything older than the current task into a summary.
2.4.guidance: Size the window for the largest conversation you expect, then add system prompt, retrieval, and headroom. Ask four separate questions: what the model needs at the start, from recent steps, on demand, and what compresses without losing decision-relevant detail.

2.5.explanation: Prompt caching saves on an unchanging prefix that is identical across requests, so stable content goes first and per-request content last — ordering is the mechanism, not configuration. Reuse across a team is a governance choice among a shared library, versioned packages, and ungoverned copying.
2.5.example: A pipeline places its long policy preamble and tool schemas before the cache breakpoint and the user's document last, so the prefix caches; a variable-first layout changes the prefix every request and never hits.
2.5.guidance: Cache only content that holds still — live state creates a consistency window that can disqualify it. Prefer versioned, self-contained packages for stable procedures that cross teams, and expect ungoverned copies to drift into slightly different behaviors.

3.1.explanation: Capability bloat is a tool set grown past what the task needs: every added tool costs tokens per request, degrades selection accuracy, and enlarges the space of actions never tested. Tools are audited the way permissions are audited, with removals recorded and reasons kept.
3.1.example: An agent configured with twelve tools misroutes calls; auditing shows four unused since launch, and removing them restores selection accuracy while shrinking the prompt.
3.1.guidance: Remove tools an agent does not need rather than relying on instructions or confirmations to steer around them. An integration carried forward out of habit from the last project is the failure to recognize.

3.2.explanation: Identity, authorization, data handling, and auditability are separate layers that fail separately. Authentication must happen server-side relative to the model call — a user asserting a role inside their own message is not identity — and authorization decides which capabilities and data this role may reach.
3.2.example: An integration injects the authenticated user's identity after login, scopes the tool's service account to that user's tenant, and passes an account reference rather than the account's sensitive fields into the context.
3.2.guidance: Filter fields by necessity — if the language task does not need the value, a reference identifier suffices. One shared key across tenants destroys attribution, and an unlogged agent action is increasingly treated as one that cannot be permitted.

3.3.explanation: Accuracy-latency trade-offs are justified per configuration decision: what quality the task requires, what latency the user or workflow tolerates, and what the cheaper option gives up. Reliability controls belong at specific layers — retries beside the call, circuit breakers at the service boundary, fallback routing with orchestration.
3.3.example: A routing classifier uses a fast model under a strict latency budget, while the rare escalation path accepts a slower, stronger model — each choice justified by the stage's tolerance, not one global setting.
3.3.guidance: Name the accuracy requirement and the latency budget separately, then show why the chosen configuration serves both. Placement of retries and fallbacks is part of the answer, not an implementation detail.

3.4.explanation: Observability at scale means instrumenting the whole path — model calls, retrieval, tools, queues, downstream services — so any request can be reconstructed afterwards. Agents need trajectory-level tracing because the trajectory is the control flow.
3.4.example: When extraction quality slides, per-stage traces show retrieval returning stale documents while the model stage performs identically — localizing the failure without replaying traffic.
3.4.guidance: Propagate one trace identifier across roles and services, and log enough to answer what the system did and why. Deferring observability until after launch fails security review as often as it fails debugging.

3.5.explanation: A RAG pipeline is designed from the corpus shape: section-numbered documents preserve structure and retrieve at the level that answers the question, prose splits on meaning boundaries, and homogeneous text takes uniform spans with overlap. Indexing, metadata, and freshness controls follow from how the corpus changes.
3.5.example: A manuals corpus keeps section structure so retrieval returns the procedure that answers the question, while an FAQ corpus uses uniform overlapping chunks — each ingestion matches its shape.
3.5.guidance: Trade retrieval precision, per-request latency, and corpus-growth cost explicitly; no setting is universally correct. Design ingestion around what parses reliably, not around what looks elegant.

3.6.explanation: Retrieval strategy matches the query pattern: keyword matching for identifier and citation lookups, semantic matching for paraphrased questions, and both run together with rank fusion when both kinds arrive — which is the usual case. Retrieval is for knowledge that holds still.
3.6.example: A policy assistant runs keyword and semantic search and merges the rankings, because engineers query by clause number while executives paraphrase — and values that change constantly are answered by a tool call to the system of record, not the index.
3.6.guidance: Recognize retrieval applied to live state by its symptoms: answers contradicting the database and staleness no embedding upgrade repairs. Match the strategy to observed queries, not to the last project.

3.7.explanation: Protocol choice turns on reuse: a direct API or SDK when one product owns the integration, a shared tool protocol such as MCP when the same tool surface must serve multiple clients, a managed runtime when the model must iterate over tools, and a coding-agent entry point only for engineer users in repositories.
3.7.example: One internal tool surfaced to both a Claude Code deployment and a support agent justifies an MCP server; the same surface behind exactly one client would buy integration cost and no reuse.
3.7.guidance: Work down the reuse list and stop at the first fit, naming which layer the question is about — entry point, build-time interface, or delivery route. Compliance obligations eliminate options before preference is discussed.

3.8.explanation: Progressive discovery stages what the model can see and reach instead of loading a monolithic tool catalog or preloaded corpus, which costs tokens on every request, degrades selection as the catalog grows, and enlarges the space of untested actions.
3.8.example: An agent starts with a search tool and loads a domain's detailed tools only when work enters that domain, so per-request tokens stay flat as coverage grows.
3.8.guidance: Let the next step pull what it needs rather than carrying every capability up front. The monolithic strategy breaks visibly as catalogs grow — selection accuracy falls before the cost does.

4.1.explanation: Evaluation metrics cover task quality, safety, security, latency, reliability, and cost, and each metric names the decision it informs. A business requirement becomes a threshold: specific behavior, a passing number set from the requirement, and failure modes enumerated as dataset categories.
4.1.example: A vague accuracy goal becomes a grounded-fact rate at or above the agreed threshold on a labeled set, latency under the published budget, and zero prohibited-content passes.
4.1.guidance: Set thresholds from the business requirement, not from whatever the prototype scored. A metric you cannot connect to a decision is telemetry, not evaluation.

4.2.explanation: Datasets mix curated cases, production samples, edge and adversarial inputs, and regression sets, while grading climbs from code-based checks through model-based judges to human review — each behavior graded at the cheapest reliable level. Judges are calibrated against human labels and use a different model than the one tested.
4.2.example: A summarization suite grades schema and length in code, scores faithfulness with a calibrated judge, and routes novel high-stakes cases to people — updating the set whenever the prompt or model changes.
4.2.guidance: Stakes decide how much you care; ambiguity decides the method — whether a prohibited action occurred is binary even when stakes are high. Prefer breadth: many cheap cases catch more regressions than a handful of meticulous ones.

4.3.explanation: A believable experiment fixes four elements before the run: a falsifiable hypothesis, random assignment consistent per user or session, one primary metric chosen in advance, and a sample size computed from the effect to detect. Shadow testing substitutes when exposure is unacceptable.
4.3.example: A prompt change runs as an A/B split with per-session assignment and grounding rate declared as the primary metric; a regulated deployment instead scores the candidate on shadowed live traffic before anyone sees it.
4.3.guidance: Statistical and practical significance differ, and a primary-metric win that degrades cost or latency may not be a win. Watch interaction effects — a change that helps typical inputs can hurt a rare-but-seasonal edge case.

4.4.explanation: Four failure classes separate cleanly: prompt failure (ambiguous instruction — fix the prompt), hallucination (fluent content with no basis — fix grounding, because wording cannot), model mismatch (the tier does not fit or changed unmeasured — re-select via evaluation), and orchestration failure (dropped or lost work — fix boundaries and tracing).
4.4.example: A support bot invents return policies: the trace shows retrieval returning nothing while the model answered anyway — a grounding failure, so the fix is a retrieval or tool change, not stronger wording.
4.4.guidance: Attribute before acting: model drift, data drift, and a model update look similar and take different fixes. Diagnose the class from the trace, then apply the fix that lives where the failure lives.

4.5.explanation: Optimization targets the tail, not the average: median latency does not breach service levels, token distributions are skewed, and aggregate dashboards hide a small request share consuming most of the budget. The levers are model selection, context size, call count, and streaming versus batch.
4.5.example: A cost spike traces to one request category whose retrieved context tripled — visible only when spend is decomposed per request rather than averaged.
4.5.guidance: Decompose per-request cost and latency alongside the aggregate view, and size the cost model on the input distribution's heavy tail. Fix the lever the decomposition points to.

4.6.explanation: Monitoring pairs collection with a feedback loop — signals, triage, decision, action, review — recorded as a table before launch: every signal with the condition that fires it, the person who acts, and the expected action. Scheduled reviews fire on a cadence, not on thresholds.
4.6.example: A deployment pairs a grounding-rate signal with a weekly owner review and a hard alert on error rate, so slow drift is caught by the cadence even when no threshold trips.
4.6.guidance: Without a mapped loop, drift runs for weeks and surfaces as a stakeholder saying the output feels less useful — every metric collected, nothing mapped to a trigger. Include slow drifts and periodic audits in the loop design.

5.1.explanation: Guardrails layer four covers: trained behavior (broad harm classes, provider-owned), system instructions (role and constraints inside one request), screening (disallowed content on the way in and out), and action authorization (whether this caller may take this action now). Each layer covers what the one below cannot.
5.1.example: An agent pairs input screening for hostile content, deterministic action authorization scoped by role, and output screening for sensitive fields — because instructions alone are not enforcement.
5.1.guidance: Screen at three points — request, response, and side-effecting action; one filter at the far end covers one point and sits downstream of the irreversible step. Choose the failure direction deliberately: where an unscreened request harms, fail closed.

5.2.explanation: The risk categories are direct prompt injection, indirect injection through retrieved content and tool results, token-budget exhaustion, tool and action abuse, and data exposure into context or logs. Walk the request path and the data path together, naming the control at every entry point.
5.2.example: A retrieval agent's dominant risk is indirect injection inside fetched documents — so documents are fenced as data, actions are gated regardless of content, and sensitive fields never enter the context window.
5.2.guidance: Indirect injection is the vector input screening never sees; the defense is structural marking plus constrained actions. The quiet failure is a rule everybody believes is enforced that exists in no layer at all.

5.3.explanation: Human review is routed by stakes — reversibility and the cost of an undetected mistake — with confidence deciding how much volume passes unsampled. Placement trades coverage against latency: approval before irreversible actions, audit after reversible ones, sampling for monitoring.
5.3.example: Refunds above a threshold require approval with the inputs, the draft, and the flagging reason attached, while low-value routings are sampled for quality rather than held.
5.3.guidance: Volume beyond what a person can read produces consent fatigue, and a bare output with one approve button leaves nothing to weigh — give reviewers the inputs, the output, and the reason. Concentrate review where it carries information.

5.4.explanation: Each obligation — GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP — becomes a control, an owner, and living evidence: which routes remain permitted, where data handling and retention are enforced, what the logs record, and who revalidates on a cadence. Choosing a compliant delivery route is a prerequisite, not proof.
5.4.example: A regulated deployment shows a countersigned agreement, the live configuration, an authorization record, and a query returning the expected retention behavior — each mapped to a named owner.
5.4.guidance: Regulations state outcomes and leave implementation to you; a design document is not evidence. A control with no owner and no artifact stops operating quietly and surfaces in an audit instead of a design review.

5.5.explanation: Unequal outcomes enter at points you own: the retrieval corpus's representation, prompt framing, few-shot example skew, and downstream routing that sends groups along different paths. Transparency serves three readers — the affected person, the regulator, and the team — from the same decision-level log, governed differently.
5.5.example: An aggregate approval rate looks healthy while one subgroup is routed to manual review more often — visible only when outcomes are segmented by group.
5.5.guidance: Instrument fairness at the four entry points rather than assuming the model arrives fair. Phrase explanations so the affected person can act, and keep the decision log minimal, retention-bounded, and access-controlled.

6.1.explanation: Discovery is structured elicitation: capture the goal in the stakeholder's own words, translate preferences into constraints, and write down assumptions before the discussion moves on. Experience words — seamless, fast, simple, intuitive — are signals to ask more, never requirements.
6.1.example: A request for a seamless handoff to agents resolves into a latency target, an integration boundary, a rule for how work passes to a person, and a failure state that exposes nothing — each buildable and measurable.
6.1.guidance: Force every statement through four categories: what the system must do, must not do, must cost, and must prove. Do not sketch architecture mid-call — the sketch's plausibility is what stops the questions.

6.2.explanation: A trade-off is presented in three elements: the benefit, the concession, and the price of undoing the choice after the rest of the system has been built on it — adding compliance posture in regulated settings. The decision travels upward as options considered, criteria weighed, recommendation, and surviving risks.
6.2.example: Recommending retrieval over fine-tuning names the quality gain, the operating cost, and what unwinding would take after ingestion and evaluation are built — the element that usually decides the room.
6.2.guidance: Open on the business consequence rather than the design, and state the limits plainly; naming them earns a security reviewer's confidence. An approval without the unwind cost is not an informed decision.

6.3.explanation: Feedback loops turn signals into decisions: every metric maps to a trigger, an owner, and an action, including scheduled reviews that fire regardless of thresholds. Service levels trace to sources — latency from user expectations, availability from business centrality, quality from evaluation criteria.
6.3.example: A handoff table pairs grounding-rate drift with a weekly owner review and a hard error-rate alert, and the sponsor receives a consumption forecast before the first invoice.
6.3.guidance: A number that traces to no source is a target someone found reasonable. Cost is the expectation most often broken by production volume — deliver the forecast and the spend-control posture early.

6.4.explanation: Documentation serves three readers at once: the inheriting engineer needs decisions and rejected alternatives, the compliance reviewer needs obligations paired with controls and evidence, and the returning architect needs dated decisions with assumptions marked as assumptions. The completeness test is whether a capable architect who missed every session could change the system safely from the document alone.
6.4.example: A decision record captures the choice and its date, the rejected options, the trade-off resolved, the owner, the evidence artifact, and whether that evidence is current.
6.4.guidance: A diagram records shape, not rationale — without rejected alternatives a successor cannot tell weighted choices from preference and will overturn a sound one. Record assumptions as assumptions, or they return as facts.

6.5.explanation: The lifecycle runs discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration, and knowing which phase a decision belongs to tells you when a phase can close. Multi-route deployments write down which surface owns which task before integration begins, or routing drifts.
6.5.example: At a handoff gate the items that belong are runbooks, owners, service levels, and monitoring scope — a proposal for new model evaluation belongs to design, however sound it would be there.
6.5.guidance: Learn the phases as an ordering, not a list: read the stem for the phase marker and reject any option that belongs to a later phase. Close with an outcome document capturing the before metric at the start — it cannot be reconstructed at the end.

7.1.explanation: Team configuration separates what shapes the agent — project instructions, packaged procedures, scoped subagents, tool servers — from what governs it: hooks, permission modes, approval flows, and sandboxing. A guarantee that must hold has to come from code and configuration, not from wording in an instructions file.
7.1.example: A team ships one shared baseline of agreed project instructions, a reviewed tool set, and a single permission posture, so configuration is reviewed and improved once instead of drifting across individual setups.
7.1.guidance: Choose distribution by reach versus governance: organization-wide availability, group-scoped packages, repository-scoped artifacts, or pinned programmatic reuse. Set spend guardrails deliberately — default model, allowed models, effort guidance, and rate caps.

7.2.explanation: AI-assisted workflows pay off where the work already happens — implementation, review, and the test cycle — rather than in a chat tab someone visits occasionally. Each stage keeps its discipline: whoever ships generated code can explain it, a flagged finding is input to judgment, and a proposed diagnosis is checked against evidence.
7.2.example: A team pairs code generation with an explicit verification checklist covering correctness, security, maintainability, and human understanding, then automates the gate so it fires on every change.
7.2.guidance: Enable one champion per team, convert a real workflow, then seed adoption in batches — lumpy adoption and stalling at basic chat are the named failure modes. Access is not adoption.

7.3.explanation: Operational support translates symptoms into causes and hands over a runbook: a gradual quality slide points at a changed model or prompt and gets the evaluation set re-run; a latency jump gets the slowest span traced; spend rising against flat usage gets the tier mix and cache behavior compared.
7.3.example: A quality slide with no deployment is diagnosed by re-running the evaluation suite and diffing results against the model version change — then the runbook records the symptom-to-action path.
7.3.guidance: Resolving one incident is firefighting; leave behind known symptom-to-action paths and an escalation map naming owners. Instrument token usage, latency, and error rate per call so a spike becomes a sortable row.
